title: Rainbows: Delighting humanity since forever
summary: Josh and Chuck explore rainbows: the history of rainbow myths and Newton's six-color (roy g biv) spectrum, how light refraction, dispersion and reflection inside raindrops create a rainbow, the 42-degree anti-solar point needed to see one, why rainbows look like arcs or full circles, double rainbows and Alexander's dark band, perspective effects that make the sky and moon look large, rainbow color proportions, and the LGBT rainbow flag. The episode ends with listener mail about the Pliny the Elder and Pliny the Younger beers.

segments.title: Opening banter and rainbow delight
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Jerry's name appearing on the Wikipedia page, then discuss how rainbows delight people, referencing the Yosemite double rainbow video, and note that rainbows have inspired myths for centuries.

segments.title: History of rainbow theory and Newton's spectrum
segments.summary: Descartes is credited with an early accurate theory of the rainbow in 1637. The hosts say Newton is associated with the color spectrum, and cite Philip Ball's Atlantic article claiming Newton's roy g biv seven-color spectrum was an interpretation, with cultures having differed on colors and Newton trying to fit light to the musical octave. Myths such as the Celtic pot of gold and the flood covenant are mentioned.

segments.title: Light speed, media and refraction
segments.summary: Using a shopping cart analogy, the hosts explain that light changes speed when moving between media, such as air, water or a prism, and that an angled transition causes bending, which is refraction.

segments.title: Dispersion inside raindrops
segments.summary: Raindrops act like prisms. Different wavelengths bend at different angles, separating white sunlight into component colors, a process called dispersion. Red bends least and violet bends most, and the light reflects and refracts again on exit.

segments.title: Viewing conditions and the 42-degree angle
segments.summary: To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you, moisture in front, and sunlight hitting the drops at about 42 degrees from the anti-solar point. The hosts explain that each raindrop sends one color toward the viewer, producing a single large rainbow.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break in the program, with no substantive content.

segments.title: Double rainbows and Alexander's dark band
segments.summary: Double rainbows come from light refracted twice, which reverses the color order in the secondary bow. Triple and quadruple rainbows are rare. The dark area between bows is Alexander's dark band, named after Alexander Aphrodisias.

segments.title: Full circle rainbows, perspective, and the moon
segments.summary: Rainbows appear as arcs because the ground blocks part of the circle; from a plane or high vantage, full circles are visible. Perspective explains why rainbows and the sky can look large or small, and the hosts explain why the moon is sometimes visible during the day.

segments.title: Rainbow color proportions and LGBT rainbow flag
segments.summary: Rainbows show more red (about 38 percent) than green (15) or blue (11). The hosts then note Gilbert Baker designed the LGBT rainbow flag, which originally had eight colors including turquoise and hot pink before fabric shortages led to six.

segments.title: Listener mail: Pliny the Elder and Younger
segments.summary: Listener Corey writes about the two Pliny beers from San Francisco breweries: Pliny the Elder, widely sold, and Pliny the Younger, a seasonal triple IPA available for two weeks a year on draft.
